result:
The morning light hit the windowsill differently that Tuesday, slanting through dust motes that had no business being so visible, so *assertive* in their tiny existences. I thought about how we never notice them until the angle is precisely wrong, until some celestial mathematics lines up to expose what was always there, floating, breathing the same air we do.

I've been thinking about inheritance lately. Not the money kind, though God knows that's its own theater of grief and awkwardness. I mean the things that pass through generations like water finding its path through limestone, slowly, inevitably, carving channels you can't see until the whole structure reveals itself hollow. My grandmother hummed while she cooked. I hum while I cook. I never chose this. Somewhere in 1953, a woman stood at a stove in Cleveland, anxious about something she never named, and the sound came out of her, unbidden, a valve releasing pressure. Now I do it. The melody changes, but the function remains. I wonder what else I do that was never mine to begin with, what anxieties I'm releasing, what pressures built in rooms I never occupied.

There's a particular silence in houses where people have recently stopped living together. You can feel it immediately, walking in—the way sound behaves differently when it doesn't have to navigate around two people's careful avoidance, or the charged space between lovers who haven't yet learned to be ex-lovers. The air gets thicker and thinner simultaneously. I stayed in a friend's apartment during his divorce, cat-sitting while he figured out temporary arrangements, and the whole week felt like being underwater. The cat knew. Cats always know. She spent the first three days hiding in the closet where his ex-wife's winter coat still hung, that specific smell of her shampoo and skin still caught in the wool, and I couldn't bring myself to move it. Some rituals of grief belong to other species. I just filled her bowl and pretended not to notice.

I want to talk about the word *liminal* but I worry it's been overused into meaninglessness, the way *journey* got co-opted by reality television and self-help Instagram. But there's no better word for certain states, for standing in doorways, for the month after graduation, for airports at 3 AM, for the breath between deciding to speak and actually speaking. We used to mark these spaces architecturally—vestibules, antechambers, the covered porch where you stomped snow from your boots before you were fully admitted. Now we pretend everything is binary, inside or outside, but we still feel the wrongness of it, the way we check our phones in elevators, that compulsive fill of a space that refuses to be one thing or another.

My neighbor grows tomatoes in five-gallon buckets on his fire escape. He's been doing this for fifteen years, through drought and deluge, through a divorce of his own, through the pandemic when he left them untended for three weeks and came back to find them somehow still alive, woody and desperate but alive. He talks to them. I've heard him, early mornings, having what sound like negotiations. *Maybe today, maybe you'll give me something today.* The tomatoes don't answer, or they answer in their own time, which is the time of plants, which is not his time, which is the whole point of the conversation. I think he's praying but can't say so directly. I think the tomatoes are his intermediaries, green and indifferent and therefore trustworthy, not like the God he was raised with who had too many opinions, too many threats attached to the love.

I read once that the human eye can distinguish between 2.3 and 7.5 million colors, depending on which study you trust and how you define *distinguish.* The range itself is interesting, that uncertainty, that we can't even agree on how much we can perceive. I think about this when I look at the sky in October, that specific blue that seems to contain the memory of all summer blues, compressed into something denser, more urgent. Is that the same blue you see? The question is unanswerable and therefore permanently interesting. We go through life making approximate translations of each other's experience, never quite arriving, never quite failing. The 2.3 million colors. The 7.5. The gap between them where most of living actually happens.

There's a bakery near my apartment where they make bread the old way, long fermentation, no shortcuts, and the owner, a woman in her sixties with flour permanently embedded in her fingerprints, once told me that the hardest part was learning to trust the process when nothing visible was happening. *The dough just sits there,* she said. *You think it's dead. You think you've failed. But it's working, even when you can't see.* I took this personally, as we take all things. I've been sitting in my own fermentation for years, apparently. The visible results are still ambiguous. Maybe I'm making bread. Maybe I'm just letting something inert become slightly less inert. The not-knowing is the practice, she didn't say but I heard.

I keep coming back to that Tuesday light, the dust motes, because it was ordinary and I was paying attention, which is the only prayer I know. The world doesn't require our attention. It persists in its complexity whether we notice or not. But something happens when we do—the reciprocity of it, the almost-recognition. For a moment the boundary thins between observer and observed, and you understand why mystics spent their lives chasing this, why they sat in caves and deserts, why they starved themselves into hallucination or simply sat so long their legs became irrelevant. Not because attention changes the world, but because it changes the one who attends, and that is the only change we can reliably make.

The grandmother again. She died without explaining the humming, without explaining much of anything. She was not a woman who explained. She was a woman who did things—planted gardens, made pie crust from lard she rendered herself, kept a loaded shotgun behind the basement door that she never once fired but checked monthly, religiously, as if the checking itself were the faith. I found her journals after, hundreds of pages of weather observations, temperatures and precipitation, nothing else. No feelings. No narrative. Just *March 14, 1978. 34 degrees. Rain.* As if the facts, accumulated, would eventually become meaning. As if meaning were something that emerged from sufficient data, a statistical significance of days.

I don't know if she was right or wrong about this. I keep my own records now, different kinds, equally incomplete. The dreams I remember. The first bird I hear each morning. Whether I felt, on waking, that the day was possible or merely obligatory. It's not enough. It will never be enough. But it's what I have, the inheritance I chose to continue, the humming in the kitchen, the attention to what persists without explanation, the Tuesday light that will come again, differently, the same, never the same, always here.
